modern_lens_framing: The Qurʾan is taken here as fixed, revealed truth; science is our provisional, evolving account of the observable world. What follows notes where the two meet — a contemplation, not a proof. Where the science later shifts, that reflects the limits of our knowledge, not the text.

86:15.title: Their Plot and God's Plot
86:15.in_short: Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ that the disbelievers are scheming against him and his message, but Allah scheme back against them and His scheme will prevail.

claims.text: The pronoun 'they' refers to the disbelievers who reject the Prophet ﷺ and the Qur'an, understood as the Meccan opponents.

sources.original_excerpt: إن هؤلاء المكذّبين بالله ورسوله والوعد والوعيد يمكرون مكرًا
ثم أخبر عن مشركي مكة
أي إن أعداء الله يكيدون كيدا أي يمكرون بمحمد
إن المكذبين للرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم، وللقرآن، يكيدون ويدبرون
كافران ئه‌وان نه‌خشه‌و پیلان دائه‌نێن

claims.text: Their scheming is aimed at defeating the truth, opposing the Qur'an's call, and hindering people from following it.

sources.original_excerpt: they plot against the people in their calling them to oppose the Qur'an
ليدفعوا بكيدهم الحق، ويؤيدوا الباطل
تكذيبهم الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم
ليدفعوا بكيدهم الحق ويؤيدوا الباطل

claims.text: al-Baghawī gives a specific angle: the disbelievers feared the Prophet ﷺ and outwardly displayed something different from what they truly held inside.

sources.original_excerpt: يخافون النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ويظهرون ما هم على خلافه

claims.text: Kayd (scheming) means a covert effort to bring harm to another, a form of makr (guile). It is only blameworthy when aimed at evil; used for a good purpose it is not condemned.

sources.original_excerpt: والكيد: العمل على إلحاق الضرر بالغير بطريقة خفية، فهو نوع من المكر
كَيد গোপনে কৌশল অবলম্বন করাকে বলা হয়

original_terms.gloss: covert scheming or strategy aimed at bringing harm

claims.text: Allah's own 'scheme' (kayd) against them is explained as istidrāj: giving them respite and letting them continue in their disbelief and disobedience from a direction they do not perceive, until He seizes them unexpectedly.

sources.original_excerpt: إملاؤه إياهم على معصيتهم وكفرهم به
وكيد الله استدراجه إياهم من حيث لا يعلمون
وقيل: كيد الله: استدراجهم من حيث لا يعلمون
إمهالهم واستدراجهم، حتى يأخذهم أخذ عزيز مقتدر

original_terms.gloss: gradually drawing someone on toward ruin by letting them proceed unaware

claims.text: An alternative reading holds that Allah's 'scheme' against them refers to what actually befell them at the Battle of Badr, killing and capture.

sources.original_excerpt: وقيل: هو ما أوقع الله بهم يوم بدر من القتل والأسر

claims.text: Allah's scheme is for the purpose of making the truth manifest and defeating falsehood, whatever the disbelievers' aversion to it.

sources.original_excerpt: لإظهار الحق، ولو كره الكافرون
لإظهار الحق، ولو كره الكافرون

claims.text: al-Saʿdī adds that this shows who truly prevails: a human being is far too weak and insignificant to out-scheme the One who is Powerful and All-Knowing.

sources.original_excerpt: فإن الآدمي أضعف وأحقر من أن يغالب القوي العليم في كيده

claims.text: Ibn Kathīr explains Allah's scheme as His arranging matters so that all the disbelievers' plots ultimately fail while success is granted to the believers.

sources.original_excerpt: I am plotting such that all disbelievers plots will fail and success will be attained by believers

claims.text: Sayyid Quṭb frames this within the surah's wider theme: Allah, who created these people from a spurting fluid and holds full mastery over their creation, guidance, death and return, is the same Power meeting their scheming. He describes the apparent contest as having, in reality, only one true Party; the second, visible party is not a genuine rival.

sources.original_excerpt: اس جنگ کا درحقیقت ایک ہی فریق ہے، دوسرا فریق جو بظاہر نظر آتا ہے وہ محض مذاق کے لئے ہے

86:15.essay_html:
These two verses turn to those who reject the Prophet ﷺ and the message he brought. "They scheme," and the commentators identify "they" as the Meccan disbelievers opposing him1,2,3,4,13,14. Their scheming is aimed at defeating the truth and blocking people from the Qur'an's call1,4,5,9,11,12,13,14. al-Baghawī (d. 1122 CE) adds a specific detail: they feared the Prophet ﷺ, yet showed outwardly something quite different from what they held inside2.

The word used for their scheming is kayd (كيد). It means a covert effort to bring harm to another, a kind of guile (makr). It is only blameworthy, some note, when directed at evil; the same word can describe a strategy used for good9,12.

Then comes the turn: "but so do I." Most commentators explain Allah's own "scheme" as istidrāj (استدراج) - giving the disbelievers rope, letting them carry on in their defiance from a direction they cannot see, until they are seized unexpectedly1,2,3,9,11,13. al-Qurṭubī (d. 1273 CE) also relays another reading: that this scheme was fulfilled at Badr, in the killing and capture that befell them there3. Ibn Kathīr (d. 1373 CE) reads it as Allah arranging matters so that the disbelievers' plots ultimately fail while success is granted to the believers4. al-Saʿdī (d. 1957 CE) and al-Muyassar add that Allah's scheme serves to bring the truth into the open, however much the disbelievers dislike it5,13.

al-Saʿdī draws out the point further: from this a person can know who truly overpowers whom. A human being, he says, is far too weak and insignificant to out-scheme the One who is Powerful and All-Knowing5. Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966 CE) reads the same idea against the whole surah's theme of creation: Allah, who brought these very people into being from a spurting fluid and holds complete mastery over their guidance, their death and their return, is the same Power now answering their plotting. He describes it as a contest with, in truth, only one real Party; the second side, though visible, is not a genuine rival6.

Whatever schemes the disbelievers weave, the sources are united that the outcome rests with the One who is far more powerful, and whose respite is never mistaken for absence1,2,3,4,5,9,13.

86:4.title: The Watcher and Man's Origin
86:4.in_short: Every soul has a watcher set over it recording and guarding it. Man is told to look at his own origin, a spurting fluid emerging from between the back and the chest, as proof that the One who first made him can bring him back.

claims.text: Reciters differed on whether 'lammā' is read with a doubled mīm (tashdīd) or lightened (takhfīf), which changes the grammar: doubled gives 'no soul but has a watcher', lightened gives 'every soul indeed has a watcher'. Al-Ṭabarī states his preference for the lightened reading as the more established Arabic usage, though he notes the doubled form is defended as a dialect of the Hudhayl tribe.

sources.original_excerpt: والقراءة التي لا أختار غيرَها في ذلك التخفيف، لأن ذلك هو الكلام المعروف من كلام العرب

original_terms.gloss: either 'indeed' (lightened) or 'except/but' (doubled)

claims.text: The verse means every soul has a guardian set over it by Allah who records and tallies its deeds, good and bad, so it can be recompensed for them.

original_terms.gloss: a guardian/watcher

claims.text: A second sense given for 'guardian' is protection: angels shield the soul from calamities, but only up to what Allah has already decreed, until the person is delivered over to those decrees.

sources.original_excerpt: حافظ من الله يحفظها ويحفظ قولها وفعلها حتى يدفعها ويسلمها إلى المقادير
الحافظ من الله، يحفظها حتى يسلمها إلى المقادير

claims.text: A hadith (relayed via al-Qurṭubī) has the Prophet ﷺ saying a believer has many angels warding off unseen harm, likened to a hand fanning flies from a bowl of honey, adding that without them the devils would snatch a person away. The number of angels is given differently in the two relays (160 in one, 360 in the other).

sources.original_excerpt: وكل بالمؤمن مائة وستون ملكا يذبون عنه

claims.text: Some held the true 'guardian' is Allah Himself, or that it is the human intellect ('aql), which guides a person toward benefit and keeps him from harm; al-Qurṭubī notes that the intellect and other means are only intermediaries, the real guardian in truth being Allah.

sources.original_excerpt: العقل وغيره وسائط، والحافظ في الحقيقة هو الله جل وعز

claims.text: The guardianship of the soul described here matches other Qur'anic verses on recording and protecting angels: the noble writers of 82:10-11, the angels before and behind in 13:11, and the watchers sent in 6:61.
Ibn Sīrīn was reported to have disapproved of the doubled (tashdīd) reading of 'lammā', exclaiming 'Glory be to Allah' when he heard it recited that way.

sources.original_excerpt: فأنكره، وقال: سبحان الله، سبحان الله

claims.text: Man, especially the one who denies resurrection, is told to look at what he was created from, because whoever was able to originate his creation is able to bring him back to life.

sources.original_excerpt: فلينظر الإنسان المكذّب بالبعث بعد الممات، المُنكر قُدرة الله

claims.text: Al-Qurṭubī explains the link to the previous verse: because a guardian records him, man is told to reflect on his own beginning so he acts in a way that pleases him at the end, not dictating to his recorder anything but what will be good for him. Al-Ṭanṭāwī relays the same connective point from al-Zamakhsharī.

sources.original_excerpt: ولا يملي على حافظه إلا ما يسره في عاقبة أمره

claims.text: 'Let him look' is explained as a call to reflective, considering observation (nazr al-mutafakkir / tadabbur), not casual glancing.

Sayyid Qutb reflects that the journey from a tiny point of fluid, with no intellect, no form, no power and no will of its own, to a fully rational human being, points to a hidden governing Hand that directs each cell, for instance ensuring the cells destined to form an eye always travel to the head and nowhere else.
The water is identified as semen (al-manī).

'Dāfiq' (spurting) is grammatically an active participle used with a passive sense, meaning 'poured/spurted' (madfūq) — a known Arabic pattern, as in the phrase 'a hidden secret' (sirr kātim) meaning 'kept secret' (maktūm).

sources.original_excerpt: يعني: من ماء مدفوق، وهو مما أخرجته العرب بلفظ فاعل، وهو بمعنى المفعول
فاعل بمعنى مفعول كقوله عيشة راضية

original_terms.gloss: spurting; grammatically active in form but passive in meaning, i.e. 'poured forth'

claims.text: Though called one water, the fluid is really the combined fluid of both man and woman, since the child is formed from both; it is spoken of as a single water because the two mix together in the womb.
A minority report attributed to Ibn 'Abbās via 'Ikrimah glosses 'dāfiq' as 'lazij' (viscous/sticky) rather than 'spurting'.

sources.original_excerpt: وعن عكرمة عن ابن عباس: دافق لزج

claims.text: The most widely relayed reading identifies 'al-ṣulb' as the man's backbone and 'al-tarā'ib' as the woman's chest area, specifically the spot where a necklace rests; the child is formed from the union of both. Ibn 'Abbās is reported (via 'Ikrimah) describing the fluid from each as yellow and fine, and that the child is born only from the union of both.

sources.original_excerpt: الترائب: موضع القِلادة

claims.text: Early exegetes recorded several other meanings for 'al-tarā'ib' besides the necklace-spot: the chest generally (Sa'īd b. Jubayr, Abū 'Iyāḍ, Ibn Zayd); the area between the shoulders and chest, or below the collarbones (Mujāhid); the hands, feet and eyes (a route from Ibn 'Abbās, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk); the man's backbone and his throat (Qatādah); the ribs below the backbone (Sa'īd); or 'the essence of the heart' from which the child comes (Ma'mar b. Abī Ḥabība). Al-Ṭabarī judges the necklace-spot reading correct, as the meaning most established in Arabic usage and supported by pre-Islamic poetry.

sources.original_excerpt: والصواب من القول في ذلك عندنا، قولُ من قال: هو موضع القِلادة من المرأة

claims.text: Al-Sa'dī considers it more likely that both 'al-ṣulb' and 'al-tarā'ib' refer to the man alone, since the 'spurting' water described is specifically the observable, felt ejaculate, which belongs to the man; and since 'tarā'ib' is properly used of men the way breasts are used of women — had the woman been meant, the verse would have said 'the backbone and the breasts'.

sources.original_excerpt: فلو أريدت الأنثى لقال: من بين الصلب والثديين

claims.text: The phrase 'from between' two things (min bayn al-ṣulb wa-l-tarā'ib) is idiomatic Arabic for 'from the two of them' (minhumā), a construction al-Ṭabarī compares to saying 'much good will come out from between these two things' meaning 'from both of them'; al-Farrā' is cited making the same point.

sources.original_excerpt: ومعنى الكلام: منهما

claims.text: Muftī Shafī' relays embryological findings suggesting seminal fluid is drawn from across the whole body via the spinal cord linking brain, loins and chest-bones, and suggests (citing al-Bayḍāwī) that the verse's mention of chest and backbone, as the body's principal front and back parts, may signify the whole body rather than assign one part to the man and another to the woman.

Sayyid Quṭb describes this water, emerging from between the back and the chest, as one of Allah's secrets, part of which he says was uncovered by scientific research over the previous half-century, understood as fluid gathering from the man's spine and the woman's upper chest-bones, meeting in a protected place; he dwells at length on the wonder of how a formless point becomes a fully organised human as evidence of a directing power.
Isrār Aḥmad states that the true source of the man's seminal fluid is between the backbone and the ribs, from where it travels to the glands designated for it.

86:4.essay_html:
Every soul, the passage says, has a watcher set over it. The commentators read the guardian two ways: a recording angel that notes every deed for the reckoning to come, or a protecting angel that wards off harm, though only up to what Allah has already decreed for that soul.1,2,3,4,5,7,9,11,12,13,14 A hadith relayed through al-Qurṭubī pictures a believer surrounded by such guardians, fending off unseen dangers the way a hand fans flies from a bowl of honey, though the two relays of the number of angels differ.3,7 Some held that the real guardian, beneath any intermediary, is Allah Himself, or even the intellect that steers a person from harm; al-Qurṭubī insists the intellect and other means are only go-betweens, the true guardian being Allah.3,9 The wording itself was read two ways by the early reciters, with a doubled or a lightened letter changing the grammar slightly, though the sense settles on the same point either way; al-Ṭabarī prefers the lightened reading as the more familiar Arabic, while noting the other is defended as a tribal dialect. One report even has Ibn Sīrīn objecting to the doubled recitation with an exclamation of astonishment.1,2,3,9

From there the sūra turns the reader toward himself. Man, especially the one who denies being raised again, is told to look at what he was made from, because whoever originated his creation the first time can certainly bring him back.1,3,4,9,13 Al-Qurṭubī reads the connection to what came before as deliberate: since a guardian is already recording him, man should reflect on his own beginning so that what gets written of him pleases him in the end.3,9 The 'looking' asked for here is not a glance but a considering, reflective gaze.2,5,9 Sayyid Quṭb, dwelling on this reflection, describes the distance travelled between a formless point with no intellect, no power, and no will, and a fully reasoning human being, as proof of a hidden Hand directing every cell to its place, so that, he notes, the cells destined to form an eye always travel to the head and never elsewhere.6

That water is named plainly: semen (al-manī), described as spurting.2,3,5,7,9,11,12,13,14 Grammatically, 'dāfiq' (spurting) is an active word carrying a passive sense, meaning 'poured forth', the same pattern found in the Arabic phrase for 'a kept secret'.1,2,3,9 Though the Qur'an speaks of one water, the commentators explain it as the fluid of both man and woman together, called one because the two mix in the womb.2,3,9,12 One minority report glosses 'dāfiq' differently, as 'viscous' rather than 'spurting'.3

The most repeated reading of where this water comes from ties 'the backbone' (al-ṣulb) to the man and 'the chest bones' (al-tarā'ib) to the woman, specifically the spot where a necklace rests on her chest, with the child formed from the union of both; Ibn 'Abbās is reported describing each fluid as yellow and fine, the child born only from their meeting.1,2,3,4,9,11,12 Early exegetes recorded a wide spread of other guesses about al-tarā'ib collected by al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī: the chest in general, the area between the shoulders and chest, the hands feet and eyes, the man's throat, the ribs beneath the backbone, even 'the essence of the heart'. Al-Ṭabarī judges the necklace-spot reading correct as the meaning most established in Arabic usage, backed by pre-Islamic poetry.1,3 Against this, al-Saʿdī offers a distinct reading: since the described 'spurting' belongs to what is felt and observed, namely the man's own emission, and since al-tarā'ib is properly a term used of men just as breasts are used of women, he judges it more likely that both the backbone and the tarā'ib belong to the man alone; had the woman been meant, he argues, the text would have said 'the backbone and the breasts'.5 Separately, the phrase 'from between' the two is noted as ordinary Arabic idiom for 'from both of them', even though it names only the two poles.1,3

Later commentators bring in what embryology has suggested. Muftī Shafī' relays research proposing that seminal fluid draws on the whole body through the spinal cord linking brain, loins, and chest bones, and wonders whether the verse's mention of chest and back, the body's two principal parts, is meant to signify the whole body rather than dividing man from woman.7 Sayyid Quṭb likewise treats the verse's mention of back and chest as one of Allah's secrets, part of which he takes recent science to have uncovered, and lingers over the wonder of a formless point becoming an organised human as a sign of a governing power.6 Isrār Aḥmad simply locates the true source of the man's fluid between backbone and ribs, from where it travels onward to its designated glands.8

Whatever the exact anatomy the words point to, the commentators keep returning to the same conclusion: the One who brought a person out of so weak and hidden a beginning is well able to bring him back.1,3,4,9,13

86:17.title: A Brief Respite for the Disbelievers
86:17.in_short: The closing verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to let the disbelievers be and grant them a short respite rather than hastening their punishment, because their reckoning is already appointed and near.

claims.text: The command "give the disbelievers respite" is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, instructing him not to hasten for their destruction but to wait for the time Allah has appointed for their punishment to fall.

sources.original_excerpt: فمهِّل يا محمد الكافرين ولا تعجل عليهم
معنى مهل وأمهل: أنظر ولا تعجل
أي أخرهم، ولا تسأل الله تعجيل إهلاكهم، وارض بما يدبره في أمورهم
meaning, wait for them and do not be in haste concerning them
فلا تستعجل لهم -أيها الرسول- بطلب إنزال العقاب بهم، بل أمهلهم وأنظرهم قليلا
تۆ مۆڵه‌ت به‌ كافران بده‌و په‌له‌یان لێ مه‌كه‌

claims.text: The word rendered "for a while" (rowaydan) is glossed two ways: Ibn ʿAbbas took it to mean "soon" (qarīban), while Qatadah took it to mean "a little" (qalīlan); both readings are transmitted without either being preferred.

sources.original_excerpt: أَمْهِلْهُمْ رُوَيْدًا يقول: قريبًا ... الرويد: القليل
رويدا أي قريبا عن ابن عباس. قتادة: قليلا
أي: قليلًا
رويدًا শব্দটি قليلًا অথবা قريبًا এর অর্থে ব্যবহার হয়েছে

original_terms.gloss: gently, a little while / soon

claims.text: Grammarians trace rowaydan to a diminutive of a root meaning to move slowly or gently, as in the image of someone walking at ease; the sense is of an unhurried, soft delay rather than abandonment.

sources.original_excerpt: والرويد في كلام العرب: تصغير رود ... كأنها ثمل يمشي على رود أي على مهل
تصغير "رُودِ" ... من قولهم: فلان يمشى على ورد، أى: على مهل، وأصله من رادت الريح ترود، إذا تحركت حركة ضعيفة

original_terms.gloss: slow, gentle movement

claims.text: Al-Qurṭubī notes that "amhilhum" functions grammatically as an emphatic restatement (tawkīd) of "mahhil" earlier in the same verse, the two forms being equivalent in meaning.

sources.original_excerpt: أمهلهم تأكيد. ومهل وأمهل: بمعنى مثل نزل وأنزل

claims.text: This command of restraint is said to have been abrogated (nasakh) by the later "verse of the sword" commanding believers to fight the polytheists; Allah seized the disbelievers at the Battle of Badr.

sources.original_excerpt: فأخذهم الله يوم بدر، ونسخ الإمهال بآية السيف
ثم نسخت بآية السيف فاقتلوا المشركين حيث وجدتموهم

claims.text: Ibn ʿAbbas described this verse as a warning (waʿīd) from Allah directed at the disbelievers.

sources.original_excerpt: هذا وعيد من الله عز وجل لهم

claims.text: The point of the respite is that the Prophet will in time see what overtakes the disbelievers of torment and destruction; this is likened to another verse: "We let them enjoy for a little while, then in the end We shall oblige them to a great torment" (31:24).

sources.original_excerpt: you will see what befalls them of torment, punishment and destruction
فسيعلمون عاقبة أمرهم، حين ينزل بهم العقاب
দেখুন তাদের শাস্তি, আযাব ও ধ্বংস কিভাবে তাদের উপর আপতিত হয়
وسترى ما يحلُّ بهم من العذاب والنكال والعقوبة والهلاك

claims.text: The granting of delay is linked to the idea of istidrāj found elsewhere in the Qur'an (7:182-183): Allah draws the wrongdoers on gradually toward ruin without their perceiving it, so the respite is itself part of a divine plan rather than mere leniency.

sources.original_excerpt: এই ঢিল বা অবকাশ দেওয়া কাফেরের পক্ষে এক প্রকার আল্লাহর কৌশল

original_terms.gloss: being drawn on gradually toward ruin without realising it

claims.text: The respite is framed as the outworking of Allah's own counter-plan (kayd) mentioned just before: the disbelievers scheme against the message, and Allah lets them proceed for a while before seizing them as One Mighty and Capable, at the moment He chooses, so the delay is strategic rather than a simple pause.

sources.original_excerpt: المراد به بالنسبة لله - تعالى -: إمهالهم واستدراجهم، حتى يأخذهم أخذ عزيز مقتدر، فى الوقت الذى يختاره ويشاؤه

original_terms.gloss: a scheme or counter-plan

claims.text: Sayyid Quṭb reads the phrasing as if the granting of respite lay in the Prophet's ﷺ own hands, though in truth the decision belongs entirely to Allah; he describes this as a style of loving, intimate address that eases the Prophet's fatigue and softens his desire for an immediate outcome.

sources.original_excerpt: یہ ایک انداز محبت ہے۔ اور اس انداز سے حضور اکرم رحمت و شفقت کے جھونکے محسوس کرتے ہیں

86:17.essay_html:
The surah ends with a direct word to the Prophet ﷺ: let the disbelievers be, and give them a short respite. The commentators agree on the core sense. He is told not to hasten their ruin, but to wait for the time Allah has appointed for the reckoning to fall.1,2,3,4,13,14 Ibn ʿAbbas called the verse itself a warning (waʿīd) aimed at the disbelievers.2

The word for "for a while" (rowaydan) carries two transmitted glosses. Ibn ʿAbbas read it as "soon", Qatadah as "a little", and both are preserved side by side.1,3,5,12 Grammarians trace the word to a diminutive of a root meaning slow, gentle movement, the image of someone walking at ease rather than being rushed.3,9 Al-Qurṭubī also notes that "amhilhum" simply restates "mahhil" for emphasis, the two words meaning the same thing.3

Some commentators add a historical note: this command to hold back was later abrogated by the verse commanding believers to fight the polytheists, after Allah seized the disbelievers at Badr.2,3

The point of the waiting is that the outcome will be seen. The Prophet is told he will witness what befalls the disbelievers of torment and ruin, a promise likened to another verse: "We let them enjoy for a little while, then in the end We shall oblige them to a great torment" (31:24).4,5,11,13 One reading ties the respite to the pattern described in 7:182-183, where Allah draws wrongdoers on by degrees toward ruin without their perceiving it, so that the delay is itself part of a plan rather than plain mercy.12 In the same vein, Ṭanṭāwī reads the respite as the working-out of Allah's own kayd (counter-plan) against the disbelievers' scheming mentioned just before, letting them proceed until He seizes them as One Mighty and Capable, at the time He chooses.9

Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966) draws attention to the address itself. It speaks as though granting the respite were in the Prophet's ﷺ own hands, though the decision belongs wholly to Allah. He reads this as a style of loving intimacy, a gentle turn of phrase that eases the Prophet's fatigue and softens the pull toward an immediate outcome.6 Isrār Aḥmad (d. 2010) places the verse within a wider pattern in the early Meccan surahs, where the Prophet ﷺ is repeatedly told not to hasten, comparable to "be patient as the messengers of firm resolve were patient, and do not hasten for them" (46:35); he reads it also as an indirect comfort to the believers then suffering at the hands of the Quraysh.8

Wahiduddin Khan (d. 2021) reads the closing verse within a broader reflection on purpose in the universe: guidance benefits only the receptive, while arrogance that refuses it is threatened with the eternal fire.10

The surah closes not with haste but with patience: a brief respite for the disbelievers, and a promise, however it is read, that what follows the delay will make plain who was right.

86:8.in_short: God who made man from a drop of fluid is well able to bring him back to life; on the Day when every hidden secret is exposed, no one will have strength of their own or anyone to help them.

86:8.essay_html:
The section closes the sūrah's argument. God who made man from a mere drop of fluid can bring him back; on the Day secrets are exposed, no one stands with their own strength or anyone to help them.

The exegetes disagree on exactly what 'bringing him back' (رجعه) means. Some read it about the fluid itself: returning it to the loins it came from, or holding it back so it never emerges, or reversing a man through the stages of life, old age to youth, youth to childhood, childhood to the sperm-drop.1,2,3 But the reading most commentators prefer, and which al-Ṭabarī (d. 923) and al-Baghawī (d. 1122) both call strongest, is that God will bring man back to life after death, resurrection itself.1,2,3,4,5,7,8,9,11,12,13,14 Al-Thaʿlabī gives the reason: the very next verse speaks of the Day secrets are exposed, showing the whole passage looks toward the Hereafter.3 Al-Māwardī raised one more possibility: that God could return the disbelievers to this world after their resurrection, since they will ask for exactly that.3

Several commentators draw out the logic behind the claim: if God brought man into being the first time from a base fluid, He is even more able to bring him back a second time. This is compared to another Qur'anic statement, that God originates creation then repeats it, and repetition is easier for Him.4,6,7,8,9,11,13 Wahiduddin Khan (d. 2021) adds that the evident ordering behind man's creation itself points to a purpose, disclosed through revelation; only a receptive person draws the lesson, while the arrogant, refusing guidance, are given over to the fire.10

'The secrets' (السرائر) are the hidden beliefs, intentions and privately done deeds no one else knew of, to be tested and laid open on the Day of Judgment.1,2,3,4,5,6,7,9,11,13,14 ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ specified these as the obligations kept privately between servant and God, prayer, fasting, ritual purification, since a person could claim falsely to have performed them.1,2,3 Asked whether ablution counted among them, Imam Mālik (d. 795) said he had only heard people say so, not a report he could rely on, though he affirmed prayer and fasting count, since either could be falsely claimed.3

Several reports are gathered around this idea. The Prophet ﷺ said every betrayer will have a flag raised behind him on the Day, naming his betrayal, a report Ibn Kathīr (d. 1373) notes is confirmed in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs.4,11,12 Ibn ʿUmar رضي الله عنه said Allah will disclose every hidden secret, radiance on some faces, gloom on others.2,3,7 Other reports describe prayer, fasting, zakat and purification as 'trusts' God has placed with His creation.3 One striking report, relayed by Ibn al-ʿArabī from Ibn Masʿūd رضي الله عنه, pictures a betrayed deposit reappearing on Judgment Day and being thrown into the depths of Hell, the person chasing it as it endlessly slips from his grasp.3 Ubayy ibn Kaʿb رضي الله عنه added that a woman is likewise entrusted with her own private affairs, her word accepted unless proven otherwise.3 On the word itself, 'tublā' (تُبلى) comes from al-balāʾ, meaning to test or try, so the secrets are exposed precisely by being tested.1,3,7,9 Al-Saʿdī (d. 1957) connects the verse to another Qur'anic scene, faces turning white and faces turning black: much stays concealed in this world, but nothing stays hidden on that Day.5

The last verse states the consequence plainly: no power, no helper. In this life, 'power' meant the backing of one's clan, and 'helper' meant an ally, as Sufyān al-Thawrī glossed the words. On that Day, neither remains.1,2,3,4,5,6,9,11,12,13,14 ʿIkrimah read the verse as reaching even kings: however much power they held in the world, they too will stand without power or helper.3 Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966) reads the whole sweep of the sūrah, the sky, the self, the stages of one's own making, ending here, as built to leave a lasting impression, precisely because some hearts still doubt even after such proofs.6

The One who first drew a person out of a drop of fluid is the same who can bring him back; on the Day every hidden thing is tested and laid open, and nothing a person once leaned on, strength or ally, will remain.

86:1.title: The Sky and the Piercing Star
86:1.in_short: Allah swears by the sky and by the night-comer (al-Ṭāriq), then names it: the piercing star (al-najm al-thāqib) whose light breaks through the dark.

claims.text: Allah opens the surah swearing by the sky and by al-Ṭāriq, the thing that comes or appears at night.

sources.original_excerpt: أقسم ربنا بالسماء وبالطارق الذي يطرق ليلا

original_terms.gloss: the night-comer; that which arrives or knocks at night

claims.text: Linguistically Ṭāriq comes from ṭaraqa, 'to knock'. In Arabic anyone or anything that arrives at night is called a ṭāriq, because a night visitor must knock to be let in. A hadith (called authentic by Ibn Kathīr) forbids a traveller from returning to his family unannounced at night for this same reason.

sources.original_excerpt: الماوردي: وأصل الطرق: الدق
the authentic Hadith that prohibits a man to come to his family Taruq

report.graded_by: Ibn Kathīr (describes it as an authentic hadith)

claims.text: The star in particular is called Ṭāriq because it is hidden by day and only appears at night, so its rising at night is itself a kind of 'knocking' or arrival.

sources.original_excerpt: يطرق بليل، ويخفى بالنهار

claims.text: A report traces the revelation of this oath to an occasion when the Prophet ﷺ was sitting with his uncle Abū Ṭālib and a shooting star lit up the sky; Abū Ṭālib was startled and asked about it, and the Prophet ﷺ told him it was a sign (āya) of Allah. Al-Kalbī's version adds details of bread and milk being shared at the time.

sources.original_excerpt: نزلت في أبي طالب...فبينما هو جالس يأكل إذ انحط نجم

report.graded_by: relayed without authentication by al-Baghawī and al-Qurṭubī

claims.text: The formula 'and what will explain to you' magnifies the greatness of the thing just sworn by. This exact phrase pattern always precedes an explanation in the Qurʾān, unlike the similar-looking 'and what will make you realise' (wa mā yudrīka), which is never followed by one — a distinction attributed to Sufyān.

sources.original_excerpt: كل ما في القرآن ( وما أدراك ) ؟ فقد أخبره به . وكل شيء قال فيه ( وما يدريك ) : لم يخبره به
قال القرطبى: قال سفيان: كل ما فى القرآن وما أدراك فقد أخبر به

claims.text: The rhetorical question signals that al-Ṭāriq is something beyond ordinary human grasp, its full significance lying past what the mind can reach on its own — which is why Allah answers the question Himself in the next verse.

sources.original_excerpt: گویا وہ ایک ایسی چیز ہے کہ انسان ادرک سے ماوراء ہے

claims.text: Allah answers His own question: al-Ṭāriq is al-najm al-thāqib, the piercing star. This explanation names the very thing sworn by.

Al-Thāqib means shining, blazing, illuminating. Ibn ʿAbbās glosses it 'the illuminating one', Mujāhid 'the blazing one', and Qatāda says its thuqūb (piercing) is its light; the same root gives the expression 'athqib nāraka', meaning light up your fire.

sources.original_excerpt: النَّجْمُ الثَّاقِبُ يعني: المضيء
أي المضيء المنير
والثاقب: المضيء...وثقوبه: ضوءه

original_terms.gloss: piercing, blazing, shining brightly

claims.text: The piercing quality of the star's light is read as its rays breaking through, or tearing, the darkness of night to reach the earth below.

sources.original_excerpt: الذي يثقب نوره، فيخرق السماوات فينفذ حتى يرى في الأرض
وہ اپنی شعاعوں کے ذریعہ تاریکیوں کو پھاڑ کر اپنی روشنی زمین پر پھینکتا ہے
المضئ الذى يثقب الظلام ويخرقه بنوره

claims.text: Commentators differ on whether al-najm al-thāqib names one specific star or is a general term for any radiant, piercing star. Some said it is al-Thurayyā (the Pleiades), a name the Arabs also called 'the star'; others said it is Zuḥal (Saturn). The majority view, however, holds it is a generic name (ism jins) covering all bright stars, with no particular star specified or required.

sources.original_excerpt: كانت العرب تسمِّي الثُّريا النجم، ويقال: إن الثاقبَ النجمُ الذي يقال له زُحَلْ
قال ابن زيد: أراد به الثريا...وقيل هو زحل
القشيري والمعظم على أن الطارق والثاقب اسم جنس أريد به العموم
والصحيح أنه اسم جنس يشمل سائر النجوم الثواقب
কোন কোন তাফসীরবিদ এর অর্থ নিয়েছেন বিশেষ করে নক্ষত্র 'সুরাইয়া'

claims.text: One report describes a specific star said to occupy the seventh heaven alone, called Zuḥal — it is said to descend among the other stars and then return to its place, being a 'knocker' both on its way down and on its way back up. This report is traced to Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan's tafsīr, and its authenticity is left an open question.

sources.original_excerpt: نجم في السماء السابعة، لا يسكنها غيره من النجوم...الله أعلم بصحتها

claims.text: A further gloss on al-thāqib links it to the shooting stars that burn or pierce the devils (shayāṭīn), attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima and ʿAṭāʾ.

sources.original_excerpt: الثاقب: الذي ترمى به الشياطين
Ikrimah said, 'It is illuminating and it burns the Shaytan'

claims.text: Sayyid Quṭb reads the whole surah as a series of intense 'blows' meant to shake a heedless soul awake. He notes that words like al-Ṭāriq, al-Thāqib, al-Dāfiq, al-Rajʿ and al-Ṣadʿ carry a sharpness in their sound and rhythm that matches their meaning.

sources.original_excerpt: یہ سورت دراصل انسان کے خوابیدہ احساس پر پے درپے شدید ضربات ہیں

claims.text: A shining star seen at night is taken as a symbolic reminder that an Observer watches over man and records his deeds, linking this oath to what follows in the surah.
A hadith reports that the Prophet ﷺ told Muʿādh, after he led a lengthy Maghrib prayer, that shorter surahs such as this one (and al-Shams) would have sufficed, so as not to burden the congregation.

sources.original_excerpt: An-Nasa'i recorded that Jabir said, 'Mu`adh lead the Maghrib prayer...'

report.graded_by: Ibn Kathīr (cites al-Nasāʾī's report without stating a grade)

86:1.essay_html:
The surah opens with an oath: by the sky, and by al-Ṭāriq, the night-comer.1,2,3,4,7,9,11,12,13,14 The word comes from a root meaning 'to knock'. In Arabic, anyone or anything that arrives at night is called a ṭāriq, because a night visitor has to knock to be let in. A hadith that Ibn Kathīr (d. 1373 CE) calls authentic forbids a traveller from returning to his family unannounced at night, for the same reason.3,4,9 The star earns this name because it hides by day and only shows itself at night, so its rising is itself a kind of arrival.1,2,3,4,9,11,12,14

One report traces the revelation of this oath to a moment when the Prophet ﷺ sat with his uncle Abū Ṭālib and a shooting star lit up the sky. Abū Ṭālib was startled and asked what it was; the Prophet ﷺ told him it was a sign of Allah. This report is relayed without its chain being vouched for.2,3

The next line asks, 'what will explain to you what the night-comer is?' Al-Qurṭubī (d. 1273 CE) notes a rule attributed to Sufyān: wherever the Qurʾān uses this exact phrase, an explanation always follows, unlike the similar phrase 'what will make you realise', which never gets one.3,9 Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966 CE) reads the question as marking something beyond what the human mind can reach on its own, which is why Allah answers it Himself.6

The answer comes at once: it is al-najm al-thāqib, the piercing star.1,4,5,7,9,13 Al-thāqib means shining, blazing, illuminating. Ibn ʿAbbās (رضي الله عنه) glossed it as 'the illuminating one', Mujāhid as 'the blazing one', and Qatāda said its piercing is its light. The same root gives the phrase 'athqib nāraka', light up your fire.1,2,3,4 Several commentators picture this piercing as the star's rays tearing through the dark of night to reach the earth.5,6,9 A further gloss links al-thāqib to the shooting stars said to burn the devils, from Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima and ʿAṭāʾ.1,3,4,14

Commentators differ over whether a specific star is meant. Some named al-Thurayyā, the Pleiades, or Zuḥal, Saturn.1,2,7,11 Al-Qurṭubī even relays a report of a star said to live alone in the seventh heaven, descending among the others and returning to its place, though he leaves its authenticity to Allah.3 The majority reading, however, treats al-najm al-thāqib as a general term for any bright, piercing star, with no single star required or named — a view al-Saʿdī (d. 1957 CE) calls the correct one.3,5,7,11

Reading the surah as a whole, Sayyid Quṭb hears it as a string of sharp blows meant to jolt a heedless soul awake, with words like al-Ṭāriq and al-Thāqib carrying that sharpness in their very sound.6 Wahiduddin Khan (d. 2021 CE) takes the shining star itself as a symbolic reminder that an Observer watches over man and keeps a record, tying this opening oath to what the surah goes on to say.10

Whichever star is meant, the commentators converge on one point: it is named for piercing the dark, and sworn by to fix the reader's attention on what only Allah can explain.

86:11.title: The Sky's Rain, the Earth's Split
86:11.in_short: Allah swears by the sky that keeps sending rain and the earth that keeps splitting open for growth, then declares that the Qur'an is a decisive word, not a jest.

claims.text: Al-rajʿ (the sky's 'return') means rain, so named because it comes back again and again, season after season.

original_terms.gloss: return/coming back — glossed as recurring rain

claims.text: Qatādah explained that the sky returns the servants' sustenance every year; without this returning rain, people and their livestock would perish.
Some held that 'the sky's return' means the sun, moon and stars, which rise from one side and set on the other, returning in a fixed cycle.
Another reading takes 'the return' to mean the angels, who return to the sky carrying the deeds of God's servants.

Al-Qurṭubī, citing the lexicographers and a line of pre-Islamic poetry, notes that raj' can mean the rain itself, or spring vegetation, and that 'dhāt al-rajʿ' has also been glossed as 'possessing benefit'.

original_terms.gloss: possessor of benefit — an alternative gloss for the rain-bearing sky

claims.text: Al-Saʿdī adds that beyond seasonal rain, the sky also 'returns' with divine decrees and matters, at every moment, not only once a year.

Sayyid Quṭb reads the rain descending and the earth splitting for plants as one pattern of life, matching the earlier scene of man's creation: fluid spurting forth, splitting through bone, and emerging from the womb's darkness. The same pattern points to the same Maker, and no one could reasonably claim to reproduce either creation.
Some commentators explain the rain's 'return' through the water cycle: sea water rises as vapour and forms clouds, which then return to earth as rain.
The earth's ṣadʿ ('splitting') is its cracking open to bring forth plants, trees and rivers.

original_terms.gloss: splitting/cracking — the earth breaking open

claims.text: Mujāhid read the 'splitting earth' differently, as mountain passes or narrow gorges like the pass at Minā, distinct from ordinary valleys.
Ibn Zayd read the splitting as the earth being broken open for cultivation and ploughing, citing the verses on rain and sprouted seed.
Others took the splitting earth to point to the resurrection, when the ground breaks open for the dead to emerge.
Isrār Aḥmad reads the rain and the sprouting plants together as sky and earth standing as joint witnesses to the truth the following verses declare.
'Innahu la-qawlun faṣl' is the answer to the oath: the Qur'an is a decisive word (faṣl) that separates truth from falsehood, guidance from error.

original_terms.gloss: a decisive word — one that separates truth from falsehood

claims.text: Ibn ʿAbbās glossed faṣl as ḥaqq, 'true'.
Qatādah glossed faṣl as ḥukm, 'a judgement' or 'a ruling'.

A report from ʿAlī (RA) has the Prophet ﷺ describing the Qur'an as a book containing news of past communities and rulings for those to come: it is al-faṣl, not a jest; whoever a tyrant abandons it is crushed by Allah, and whoever seeks guidance elsewhere is led astray.

report.graded_by: not graded by al-Qurṭubī or Muftī Shafīʿ in the cited passage

claims.text: Al-Qurṭubī notes a further possibility: 'the decisive word' may refer specifically to the earlier warning in the surah, that He is able to bring man back, on the day secrets are tested, rather than to the whole Qur'an.
'Wa mā huwa bil-hazl' means the Qur'an is not play, jest, or falsehood, but wholly serious and true.

original_terms.gloss: jest or frivolity, opposite of jidd (seriousness)

claims.text: Ibn ʿAbbās glossed 'not hazl' as 'not bāṭil', not falsehood.
Mujāhid glossed hazl as laʿb, mere play.
Al-Saʿdī expands that this is the word which separates between factions and their claims, and by which disputes are settled.
Rebar's Kurdish tafsir reads this verse together with the previous one as evidence that the Qur'an is God's actual speech, and not something created.

Wahiduddin Khan reads the section as showing evident design in the sky and the earth, implying a purpose behind creation that has been disclosed through revelation. Only the receptive learn from it; the arrogant who reject guidance are said to face the fire.
Al-Muyassar notes that a created being may not swear by anything other than Allah; to do so would be shirk (associating partners with Allah). Only Allah may swear by His own creation.

86:11.essay_html:
The passage swears by two ordinary sights, rain falling from the sky and plants breaking through the ground, to back up one claim: the Qur'an is a decisive word, and no joke.

The sky is called “dhāt al-rajʿ”, the one ‘of return’. Most commentators take this as rain, named for its habit of coming back season after season.1,2,3,4,5,7,9,11,12,13,14 Qatādah adds a practical note: this returning rain carries the servants' yearly provision, and without it people and their livestock would not survive.1,4,11 A minority reading takes the ‘return’ to mean the sun, moon and stars cycling round the sky,1,3,9 or the angels returning to heaven with the deeds of God's servants.3,9 Al-Qurṭubī (d. 1273 CE), citing the lexicographers and a line of old Arabic poetry, notes raj' can also simply mean the rain itself, or spring growth, and that the phrase has been read as ‘the possessor of benefit’.3 Al-Saʿdī (d. 1957 CE) widens the picture further: the sky also ‘returns’ with divine decrees at every moment, not only with the yearly rain.5

Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966 CE) draws out a pattern: rain falling and plants splitting the soil mirror the earlier scene of man's own making, fluid spurting forth, splitting through bone, emerging from the womb's darkness. One pattern, one Maker, and none can claim to copy either.6 Some later commentators explain the rain's ‘return’ through the water cycle itself: sea water rising as vapour, then falling again as rain.11,12

The earth is called “dhāt al-ṣadʿ”, the one ‘of splitting’. The common reading is that it cracks open to bring forth plants, trees and rivers.1,2,3,4,5,8,9,11,12,13,14 Mujāhid instead read it as mountain passes, like the narrow pass at Minā.1,3 Ibn Zayd read it as land broken open for ploughing and cultivation.1,3 Others took the splitting earth to point ahead to the resurrection, when the ground breaks for the dead to rise.3,5,12 Isrār Aḥmad (d. 2010 CE) reads sky and earth together as witnesses standing behind the truth the next verses state.8

The oath's answer comes in verse 13: this, meaning the Qur'an, is “qawlun faṣl”, a decisive word that separates truth from falsehood.1,2,3,4,5,7,9,11,12,13,14 Ibn ʿAbbās glossed faṣl as ḥaqq, true; Qatādah glossed it as ḥukm, a ruling.1,4 A report traced to ʿAlī (RA) has the Prophet ﷺ describing the Qur'an as a book carrying news of the past and rulings for what follows, itself al-faṣl, no jest, warning that whoever a tyrant abandons it is crushed and whoever seeks guidance elsewhere is led astray.3,7 Al-Qurṭubī also notes the ‘decisive word’ could point back more narrowly to the surah's own earlier warning about man's return and the testing of secrets.3

Verse 14 seals the point: the Qur'an is “not al-hazl”, not play, jest or falsehood.1,2,4,5,7,9,11,12,13,14 Ibn ʿAbbās read ‘not hazl’ as ‘not bāṭil’, falsehood; Mujāhid read hazl simply as laʿb, play.1 Al-Saʿdī adds that this is the word by which factions and their claims are separated and disputes settled.5 Rebar's tafsir reads verses 13 and 14 together as pointing to the Qur'an being God's actual speech, not something created.14

Wahiduddin Khan (d. 2021 CE) reads the whole passage as showing design in creation, implying a purpose disclosed through revelation, received by the receptive and rejected by the arrogant.10 Al-Muyassar adds a note on the oath itself: a created being may not swear by anything other than Allah, only Allah may swear by His own creation.13

Rain that keeps returning and earth that keeps splitting for life are set, in these commentaries, beside a word the sources call equally certain, equally alive, and not to be taken as a jest.
